syllabus.clause: "Arc::clone is cheap" stops being true under contention: every clone and drop is an atomic read-modify-write on a shared cache line

items.item: Every time we call Rc::clone, the reference count to the data increases, and the data won't be cleaned up unless there are zero references to it

at.step: A shared count, cheap to touch

items.item: The call to Rc::clone only increments the reference count, which doesn't take much time, unlike a deep copy

at.step: A shared count, cheap to touch

items.item: Arc<T> uses atomic operations for its reference counting, which is what makes it thread-safe

at.step: The same shape, safe across threads

items.item: Atomic operations are more expensive than the ordinary memory accesses Rc<T>'s plain count uses

at.step: Measuring what contention really costs

items.item: Rc<T> is a safe default because the compiler catches any attempt to send one between threads

at.step: Moving Rc into a new thread

items.item: Box, Rc, and Arc all point at the same kind of heap allocation; the only thing that changes between them is how many owners are allowed to hold a pointer to it and whether touching the owner count is safe from more than one thread

at.step: One owner, many owners, many owners safely

items.item: Rc's non-atomic count is not a missing feature; it is a deliberate optimization, because most shared data never leaves one thread, and paying for atomics on every single-threaded clone would be pure waste

at.step: A shared count, cheap to touch

items.item: The compiler rejects moving an Rc across threads at compile time, specifically because Rc does not implement Send; this is caught before the program ever runs, not as a runtime panic or a data race caught by luck

at.step: Moving Rc into a new thread

items.item: Arc being Send and Sync is conditional on its contents also being Send and Sync; wrapping a non-thread-safe type in Arc does not retroactively make that type's own interior safe to share, only the pointer and count around it

at.step: The same shape, safe across threads

items.item: A real contention measurement needs every thread to start touching the shared count at genuinely the same moment, not just be spawned around the same time; without a barrier, thread startup jitter can hide the very contention the benchmark is trying to show

at.step: Does splitting the work across threads speed it up?

items.item: The naive expectation that four threads finish a fixed amount of work in a quarter of the time only holds when the work is actually independent; an atomically-shared counter makes every thread's clone and drop contend for the exact same cache line, destroying that independence

at.step: Does splitting the work across threads speed it up?

items.item: This topic measured the contended run finishing well above even the single uncontended thread's own total time, not just above the naive quarter-time prediction, which is the stronger and more surprising claim worth taking away

at.step: Measuring what contention really costs

items.item: The measured cost here is cache-line contention and atomic retry overhead, not heap allocation; the same Arc's single backing allocation is shared throughout, so none of the extra time comes from allocating or freeing memory

at.step: Measuring what contention really costs

items.item: This topic reuses the same compare-and-swap-flavored cost that Chapter 1's arc-mutex-reflex smell gestured at without measuring; here the atomic refcount itself, with no Mutex involved at all, is enough to show a real, measured slowdown under contention

at.step: Measuring what contention really costs

items.item: Choosing Rc over Arc is not just about whether data crosses a thread boundary today; it is a standing commitment that it never will without a later, deliberate type change, which is exactly why the compiler enforces it rather than leaving it to convention

at.step: Recap: one owner, shared, and shared safely
